nature-acct-021.title: Human development: growth as a means, not the goal
nature-acct-021.text: Aristotle noted that wealth is merely useful for something else, not the good being sought. Human development takes that idea seriously. It is a view of progress that widens economic development to include social, political and even ethical dimensions. The UN Development Programme defines it as enlarging people's choices. These include the chance to live a long, healthy life, to be educated, to have a decent standard of living and to enjoy freedom and self-respect. On this view economic growth ({{ref:nature-econ-478}}) is only a means of enlarging those choices, not the goal itself. The idea grew in the 1980s from Amartya Sen's capabilities perspective ({{ref:nature-econ-182}}), with Mahbub ul Haq among its key early figures. Its six pillars are equity, sustainability, productivity, empowerment, cooperation and security. The UN's Human Development Reports carry several indices built on it, including gender indices and {{ref:nature-acct-003}}, which stems directly from this work.

nature-acct-003.title: Human Development Index: ranking countries by people's lives
nature-acct-003.text: Since 1990 the UN's Human Development Reports have tried to move development economics away from national income accounting and towards people-centred policies. Their best-known tool is the Human Development Index, or HDI. It is a single score combining life expectancy, schooling and income per person, used to sort countries into four tiers of human development. It rests on Amartya Sen's capability idea: whether people are able to 'be' and 'do' desirable things, such as being healthy or taking part in community life. Since 2010 it has combined life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and gross national income per person at purchasing power parity. Each dimension is scaled to an index between 0 and 1. The HDI is their geometric mean, found by multiplying the three scores and taking the cube root. Critics fault it for neglecting sustainability, inequality and democracy. In response came {{ref:nature-acct-005}} and a planetary pressures-adjusted HDI. One study found 11%, 21% and 34% of countries could be misclassified by data updates, formula revisions and arbitrary thresholds.

nature-acct-018.title: Gross National Happiness: Bhutan's rival to GDP
nature-acct-018.text: In 1972 Bhutan's fourth King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, declared Gross National Happiness more important than GDP. GNH is now a philosophy followed by Bhutan's government, with an index that measures a population's collective happiness and well-being. It rests on four pillars: fair socio-economic development, environmental conservation, preserving culture and good governance. Nine domains sit alongside them, including ecological diversity and resilience. Each domain mixes survey answers with objective indicators, and people are classed as happy or not-yet-happy by their scores. Bhutan's 2008 Constitution made the GNH Index an official goal, and screening tools test new policies and projects against it. In 2011 a UN General Assembly resolution urged members to follow Bhutan and measure happiness and well-being. Versions of the survey have been used in Victoria in Canada, in Seattle and in Vermont. Opinion is divided. Critics call GNH a propaganda tool that distracted from Bhutan's expulsion of its Nepalese Hindu minority and from the hardship of many Bhutanese. Others see it as an evolving, more democratic development philosophy.

nature-acct-007.title: Beyond GDP: the search for better scorecards
nature-acct-007.text: Bhutan was among the first. Its Gross National Happiness Index was one of the earliest national attempts to judge progress by more than output. Similar projects followed, such as the UK's measure of national well-being. Together they form the push known as Beyond GDP. It is the effort to build broad measures of economic well-being that go further than GDP and other national income figures ({{ref:nature-econ-498}}). Approaches include the European Union's Beyond GDP programme, the OECD's Better Lives indicators and many alternative measures of wellbeing or happiness. The European Commission sorts the alternatives into five groups. The first is GDP itself. Enlarged GDP measures subtract costs such as environmental degradation, the using up of resources or higher income inequality. Social indicators, measures of the environment and measures of well-being make up the rest. The movement splits on ambition. Some proposals aim to replace GDP outright. Many others aim to supplement it with a 'dashboard' of metrics for the economy and well-being. The World Bank suggests three alternatives to GDP: the HDI, Gross National Happiness and {{ref:nature-acct-026}}.

nature-acct-010.title: Green GDP: subtracting the damage from growth
nature-acct-010.text: Fell a forest for timber and GDP records the output, not the loss. GDP measures output alone and ignores the running down or replenishment of the wealth behind it, so it cannot tell whether income is sustainable. Green GDP is a measure of growth that subtracts the environmental consequences of that growth from ordinary GDP. In simple form, green GDP equals GDP minus environmental costs minus social costs. Environmental costs include the using up of resources such as oil and timber, ecological damage such as topsoil erosion, and restoration costs such as restoring wetlands. Benefits from forests, wetlands and farmland stay hidden in GDP because they are hard to measure and price. The UN's system for environmental accounts, SEEA ({{ref:nature-found-013}}), makes it possible to build full accounts from which green GDP can be derived and compared between countries. In the US, early green accounts in 1994 showed GDP overstated mining's contribution to national wealth, and a 1995 amendment halted the work. Experts still disagree on whether to adjust the existing national accounts or redefine income. They also dispute whether non-market goods such as ecosystem services can be reliably valued. Stiglitz, Sen and Fitoussi argued that green GDP does not measure sustainability itself.

nature-acct-015.title: Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission: France asks what to measure
nature-acct-015.text: In 2008 the French government set up an inquiry into how a nation's wealth and social progress could be measured without relying on the one-dimensional GDP figure. Its formal name was the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress, but it became known by its three leading figures. Joseph Stiglitz chaired it, Amartya Sen was economic adviser and Jean-Paul Fitoussi was coordinator. The final report came out in September 2009. It proposed a well-being framework covering health, environment, work, physical safety, economic safety and political freedom. It also took aim at green GDP ({{ref:nature-acct-010}}) and similar indices. These only charge GDP for environmental damage, the report argued, and do not measure sustainability as such.

nature-acct-012.title: Inclusive wealth: counting every kind of capital
nature-acct-012.text: From 1990 to 2014, inclusive wealth across 140 countries rose 44%, about 1.8% a year. That sounds healthy until it is broken down per person. In 44 of the 140 countries, inclusive wealth per person fell after 1992, even as GDP per person rose in nearly all of them. That is a sign that nature was being used up unsustainably. Inclusive wealth is the total value of every kind of capital in a place, including human, social, public and natural capital. Unlike GDP, the Inclusive Wealth Index lets countries check whether they are developing in a way that lets future generations meet their own needs. UNEP developed it with Kyushu University. It estimates the amounts of human, natural and produced capital, the productive base of an economy. Natural capital here includes farmland, forests and fisheries, which renew, and fossil fuels and minerals, which do not. The change in wealth sums the changes in each kind of capital, each weighted by its shadow price: the estimated price of something with no market price. Using shadow prices for nature is called controversial, because knowledge of how life-supporting ecosystems produce value has gaps. Globally, produced capital per person has grown most, often at the expense of natural capital.

nature-acct-013.title: Wellbeing economy: designing policy around people and nature
nature-acct-013.text: In 2021 Scotland, New Zealand, Iceland, Wales, Finland and Canada formed the Wellbeing Economy Governments partnership, or WEGo. Each had adopted the wellbeing economy as national policy. A wellbeing economy is a public policy framework in which the economy is designed to serve social, health, cultural, fairness and nature outcomes. Its aim is to move beyond GDP as the main measure of how well a national economy is doing. Several countries now use wellbeing metrics to guide policy and budgets, focusing on education and skills, health, gender and inclusion. The World Health Organization has adopted wellbeing as a whole-of-government approach, first set out in the 2021 Geneva Charter for Wellbeing. The Wellbeing Economy Alliance, founded in 2018, is the leading network of organisations and movements working towards it. Support is broad: an Ipsos survey in 17 of the G20 countries found 68% of respondents favoured putting wellbeing ahead of profit. Wellbeing economics is grouped with {{ref:nature-eecon-146}}, {{ref:nature-eecon-072}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-143}} under the umbrella of {{ref:nature-eecon-158}}.

nature-acct-019.title: Happiness economics: measuring what people feel
nature-acct-019.text: Classical and neoclassical economists treated happiness as something that could not be measured. Happiness economics is described as a radical break with that tradition. It studies happiness, well-being, life satisfaction and quality of life, linking economics with psychology, sociology and health. Instead of wealth, income or profit, it treats happiness and quality of life as the thing to maximise. Researchers measure it with self-reported surveys and with objective measures such as lifespan, income and education. One finding stands out. Once wealth reaches subsistence level, enough to cover basic needs, extra wealth adds much less to well-being. In 2010 Kahneman and Deaton found that day-to-day emotional well-being rose with household income only up to about $75,000 a year, though life satisfaction kept rising. Direct happiness surveys are increasingly used instead of GDP or GNP to judge whether policies succeed. Critics worry that happiness metrics may serve political or even authoritarian goals, and that survey scales distort results through 'rounding'.

nature-acct-022.title: OECD Better Life Index: build your own measure of progress
nature-acct-022.text: The OECD Better Life Index lets its users decide what matters. Launched in May 2011, it measures several dimensions of economic and social progress beyond GDP. It grew out of the concern of {{ref:nature-acct-015}} that GDP failed to give a true picture of people's current and future well-being. It covers 11 topics, including housing, income, jobs, community, education and environment, each built from 1 to 4 measures. Users rank each topic from 0 to 5 by importance to build their own index, and the OECD reports the pooled results in its How's Life? report. Critics say it misses things such as social networks and freedom of speech, and question its relative scoring.

nature-acct-023.title: Social Progress Index: progress measured without money
nature-acct-023.text: Denmark and the United States have similar GDP per person. Yet Denmark scores 10 points higher on the Social Progress Index. Created in 2013 by the Social Progress Imperative, the index measures the real-life outcomes people experience across many social and environmental measures. Unlike other Beyond GDP measures, it deliberately leaves out every indicator of economic performance. It defines social progress as meeting basic human needs, building blocks for a better quality of life, and the chance for people to reach their full potential. Its founders created it because they found the HDI and happiness indices insufficient.

nature-acct-026.title: Adjusted net saving: is a nation getting richer or poorer?
nature-acct-026.text: Ordinary saving figures miss what a country uses up. Adjusted net saving, also called {{ref:nature-eecon-220}}, corrects for that. It takes ordinary net saving ({{ref:nature-econ-587}}), subtracts the value of resources used up and environmental damage, and adds investment in human capital. The result is the net change in a nation's produced, natural and human capital, valued in money. The idea grew from {{ref:nature-eecon-223}}, as Pearce, Atkinson and Hamilton set out a measure of net investment across kinds of capital. A positive value is linked to the possibility of long-run sustainability, so policy should aim to keep it at or above zero. The World Bank publishes these estimates for over 150 countries as 'adjusted savings' and suggests them as an alternative to GDP. Along with accounts of humanity's demand on nature ({{ref:nature-acct-027}}), it is an example of an index focused on consuming more than nature can sustain ({{ref:nature-eecon-185}}).

nature-acct-011.title: China's green GDP experiment and its collapse
nature-acct-011.text: In 2004 China announced it would judge its top officials by green GDP instead of ordinary GDP. The first report, for 2004, put the financial loss from pollution at 511.8 billion yuan ($66.3 billion), or 3.05 percent of the economy. The experiment did not survive its own numbers. Environmental adjustments cut growth to politically unacceptable levels, nearly zero in some provinces. The 2005 report was suppressed, and in 2007 the effort collapsed. Its failure is linked to a mismatch between central authorities and local governments.

nature-acct-008.title: The 2007 Beyond GDP conference and the EU's response
nature-acct-008.text: In 2007 more than 650 policy makers, experts and social activists gathered for the 'Beyond GDP' conference. The European Commission, European Parliament, OECD, WWF and {{ref:nature-hist-026}} hosted it to seek wider measures of progress to guide policy. The EU followed with a communication, 'GDP and beyond', that set five actions. They included complementing GDP with environmental and social measures and extending national accounts to environmental and social issues. Results included the EU's first quality-of-life indicators and backing for UN adoption of SEEA as the international standard.

nature-acct-009.title: Britain's programme for measuring national well-being
nature-acct-009.text: In 2010 the UK set out to measure how its people are doing, not only what they produce. The Measuring National Well-being programme, led by the Office for National Statistics, aims to build trusted measures of the nation's well-being. Its well-being wheel has headline indicators for health, relationships, job satisfaction, economic security, education, environment and people's own rating of their well-being. It has also published experimental work, such as household satellite accounts, side accounts kept alongside the main national accounts, that put a value on unpaid household production.

nature-acct-014.title: New Zealand's Wellbeing Budget puts people before growth
nature-acct-014.text: In May 2019 New Zealand presented its first budget built around people's wellbeing and the environment rather than GDP alone. Prime Minister Ardern argued that citizens' health and life satisfaction, not wealth or growth, should be the measure of a country's progress. The budget chose five priorities: climate and environment, productive work, Maori and Pacific opportunities, child wellbeing, and mental and physical health. The approach did not outlast the government that made it. The next, National-led coalition government dropped it in 2024.

nature-acct-025.title: Environmental functions: when nature's uses compete
nature-acct-025.text: Water can serve as drinking water or as a dumping ground for waste, but once pollution passes a threshold, the two uses compete. Each is an environmental function: a possible use of the physical surroundings people did not make, on which they depend for producing, consuming, breathing and recreation. When one use comes at the expense of another, the functions compete. Competing functions are scarce, and so they are economic goods ({{ref:nature-found-051}}). Most functions that were once free goods, so plentiful that using them cost nothing, have become scarce.

nature-acct-024.title: Sustainable national income: what nature could support for ever
nature-acct-024.text: What if an economy produced only as much as nature could support for ever? Sustainable national income, or SNI, puts a number on that. It estimates the highest production level at which, with that year's technology, vital environmental functions stay available for ever. Economist Roefie Hueting developed the framework, working with a multidisciplinary team at Statistics Netherlands for nearly forty years. Ordinary national income leaves out the loss of environmental functions, so it is always higher than the SNI. The gap between the two shows how far production is from sustainability: a shrinking gap means progress, a growing one means drifting away. Following the rule of erring on the side of caution ({{ref:nature-pol-201}}), the SNI assumes no technological progress during the shift to sustainability. The estimates are stark. Tinbergen and Hueting's rough 1991 world estimate put sustainable income at 50 percent of world production. A 2001 estimate for the Netherlands also came to around 50 percent of national income, about the production level of the early 1970s. Between 1990 and 2000 the Dutch gap grew by about 10 billion euros.

nature-acct-020.title: The Easterlin paradox: richer nations, no happier?
nature-acct-020.text: Within a country, richer people report more happiness than poorer ones. Yet as a nation's average income grows, average happiness does not seem to rise. That puzzle is the Easterlin paradox. Richard Easterlin formulated it from survey results comparing happiness and GDP across and within countries. Across nations there is a significant link between GDP and happiness, which some researchers in 2002 said holds only up to about $15,000 GDP per person. Whether the paradox holds at all is disputed. Several studies in the 2000s found the opposite, and more robust research links economic development with population well-being.

nature-acct-005.title: Inequality-adjusted HDI: development as people actually live it
nature-acct-005.text: An average can hide a great deal. The inequality-adjusted HDI, or IHDI, introduced in the 2010 Human Development Report, discounts the HDI for inequality ({{ref:nature-econ-494}}) to show the actual level of human development. The plain HDI then reads as the potential: the maximum human development a country could reach if there were no inequality. The IHDI and the Gender Inequality Index were both adopted in 2010, growing out of the capability approach.

nature-acct-004.title: Measure of Economic Welfare: Nordhaus and Tobin's correction
nature-acct-004.text: Nations that eat up their capital are worse off than their income suggests. {{ref:nature-hist-050}} and James Tobin made that argument in 1972, insisting that welfare must be sustainable. Their Measure of Economic Welfare, or MEW, was the first model to estimate households' real yearly consumption as a welfare measure. It belongs to a family of welfare indices, with Japan's Net National Welfare in 1973 and {{ref:nature-acct-001}} in 1989, that add positive and negative nonmarket items to national accounts. Clifford Cobb and John Cobb later argued that the MEW failed to include the running down of natural capital.

nature-acct-017.title: Green national product: fixing GNP's backward ledger
nature-acct-017.text: Pollute, then clean up, and GNP, the gross national product, counts both as gains. Critics say this puts the environment on the wrong side of the ledger. GNP lumps together spending that makes people worse off, keeps them in place or makes them better off. The single figure gives no clue about real progress. {{ref:nature-hist-040}} argued that GNP ignores a basic business accounting rule: all revenues and expenses are allocated to income. The green national product responds by folding environmental degradation and the using up of resources into a country's national product. The line of welfare adjustments runs from the MEW to {{ref:nature-acct-001}} in 1989 and {{ref:nature-acct-002}} in 1995, which also adjusts for housework, volunteering, crime and leisure.

nature-val-104.title: Defensive expenditures: when fighting harm counts as growth
nature-val-104.text: Money spent rebuilding destroyed homes counts in GDP exactly like money spent on new production. In accounts for the environment, spending meant to limit possible damage to oneself is called a defensive expenditure. Standard accounts do not subtract this spending to fight 'bads'. It counts as if it were a gain. {{ref:nature-acct-001}} corrects for this: it subtracts private defensive spending and counts only non-defensive public spending. Such spending also carries information. What people pay to protect themselves from pollution can reveal how much they value avoiding it ({{ref:nature-val-087}}).

nature-acct-001.title: Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare: GDP with the costs taken out
nature-acct-001.text: From 1950 to 1986, US GDP kept growing. Yet by one calculation, average economic welfare levelled off after the 1970s. That calculation was the Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare, or ISEW, developed in 1989 by ecological economist {{ref:nature-hist-040}} and theologian John B. Cobb as a more valid measure of progress than GDP. Instead of just adding up spending, it weighs consumer spending against income distribution and the costs of pollution and other unsustainable practices. Its rough formula starts with personal consumption and adds public non-defensive spending, capital formation and household labour services. It then subtracts private defensive spending, environmental degradation costs and the depreciation of natural capital. Cobb and Daly blamed two things for production gains not turning into welfare gains: the side effects of production and unequal income distribution. The ISEW has since been compiled for many other places, including the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Chile, Poland, Pakistan and China. Like GDP, it boils welfare down to one number, but it puts social and environmental issues into the sum in money terms.

nature-acct-002.title: Genuine progress indicator: counting pollution as a loss
nature-acct-002.text: GDP counts pollution twice as a gain: once when it is made and again when it is cleaned up. The genuine progress indicator, or GPI, counts it as a loss, roughly equal to its clean-up and damage costs. The GPI is a measure proposed to replace or supplement GDP by counting the environmental and social factors GDP leaves out ({{ref:nature-found-031}}). It grew out of later work extending the ISEW, with extra emphasis on welfare and the ecological sustainability of the economy. Its foundation is John Hicks's idea of sustainable income: what can be consumed in one period without reducing consumption in the next. In simplified form, it takes consumption weighted by income, adds non-market services, subtracts defensive costs and nature's deterioration, and adds capital growth and the trade balance. As of 2014, Vermont, Maryland, Washington and Hawaii had passed state initiatives to consider it in budgeting. Statistics Finland's series from 1945 to 2011 showed GDP and GPI rising together in the 1970s and 1980s, then diverging after the early-1990s recession. Critics say it is harder to measure, rests on a contested definition of well-being and invites political manipulation. Whether growth in money terms hides lost well-being is called a main issue between green and neoclassical economists.

openers.acct: GDP adds up what a country produces, but it does not ask what that production costs in health, happiness or nature. This part of the course is about measuring wealth and progress more honestly. Some measures widen the lens to people's lives: {{ref:nature-acct-003}} scores life expectancy, schooling and income, and Bhutan's {{ref:nature-acct-018}} sets out to measure collective happiness. Others put nature on the books: {{ref:nature-acct-010}} subtracts environmental damage from GDP, and {{ref:nature-acct-012}} counts natural capital alongside human and social capital. Together they ask whether an economy is truly growing richer or simply spending down what it owns.
openers.beyond-gdp: In 2008 the French government set up an inquiry, {{ref:nature-acct-015}}, into how a nation's progress should be measured. It joined a broad push known as {{ref:nature-acct-007}}. Some answers measure people's lives directly: {{ref:nature-acct-019}} studies life satisfaction, while {{ref:nature-acct-022}} and {{ref:nature-acct-023}} track many social and environmental outcomes at once. Others adjust the accounts: {{ref:nature-acct-026}} subtracts resource depletion and environmental damage from what a nation saves. A {{ref:nature-acct-013}} goes furthest, designing policy itself around health, fairness and nature.

reviews.beyond-gdp: The measures in this chapter share one complaint: GDP counts output but not what output costs. Some widen the view to people's lives, from the HDI's mix of life expectancy, schooling and income to Bhutan's Gross National Happiness and the surveys of happiness economics. Others put nature into the accounts: green GDP, the ISEW and the GPI subtract pollution and depletion, while adjusted net saving and inclusive wealth ask whether a nation's stock of capital is shrinking. Sustainable national income goes furthest, and two rough estimates put it at about half of actual output. China's abandoned green GDP and New Zealand's dropped Wellbeing Budget show that a better measure is easier to design than to keep.
